chasing_ghosts.title: Chasing Ghosts: Instruction Following as Bayesian State Tracking
chasing_ghosts.authors: Peter Anderson; Ayush Shrivastava; Devi Parikh; Dhruv Batra; Stefan Lee
chasing_ghosts.problem: Follow an R2R route using RGB-D panoramic views, camera calibration and known pose. The 'ghost' is an imagined demonstrator whose instruction-conditioned location is inferred; it is not a generated future camera image or the physical agent's uncertain localization.
chasing_ghosts.mechanism: Sections 3–4 pp. 3–6: CNN features are projected using depth into a ground-plane map M in R^(C×Y×X), updated by sparse convolutional GRU. An LSTM instruction decoder emits successive action and observation descriptions. A differentiable histogram Bayes filter represents ghost pose (x,y,heading). The motion update convolves the previous belief with instruction/map-dependent normalized kernels (Eqs.3–4); a LingUNet observation likelihood multiplies this prior and the posterior is renormalized (Eq. 5). Six inner filter steps infer the whole instruction trajectory and are rerun whenever the real agent expands its map. A separate MLP scores observed graph nodes using belief neighborhood, distance and visited flag; selecting a visited node stops. Training minimizes KL to demonstrated instruction-trajectory beliefs plus teacher-action cross-entropy, with a 50:50 teacher/policy mixture; visual CNN is frozen. Inference repeatedly maps real views, reinfers the ghost's endpoint and chooses reachable nodes. No online model gradients or RGB synthesis.
chasing_ghosts.novelty: Turns instruction following into structured probabilistic localization of a hypothetical demonstrator, combining geometric mapping, language-conditioned motion and observation models. Relative to LingUNet endpoint prediction, explicitly represents sequence and orientation. It is prior art for multimodal navigation beliefs, not empirical probability calibration.
chasing_ghosts.results: Table 1 p. 7: unseen goal localization 44.9% versus LingUNet 32.2%; removing heading yields 39.4%. This supports the filtering representation. Table 2 p. 8: complete navigation unseen SR 35/SPL 31 and test 33/30; the complete agent is weaker than strong contemporary navigation baselines. Better localization does not establish better control. Standard R2R split, no independent run.
chasing_ghosts.bottleneck: Known accurate poses/depth and discretized ground-plane map restrict transfer; fixed six ghost steps compress variable instructions. Bayesian normalization does not validate learned likelihood calibration or independence assumptions. The strong goal-localization versus weaker end-to-end navigation result exposes a planning/control interface bottleneck. Later topological systems improve navigation, but do not directly test whether a persistent multimodal belief helps under ambiguous instructions.
chasing_ghosts.followups: DUET/topological mapping changes the controller and representation; HNR and SALI add predicted future content. A direct matched comparison preserving multimodal belief versus collapsing it remains absent in this reviewed chain.

cotvla.title: CoT-VLA: Visual Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models
cotvla.authors: Qingqing Zhao; Yao Lu; Moo Jin Kim; Zipeng Fu; Zhuoyang Zhang; Yecheng Wu; Zhaoshuo Li; Qianli Ma; Song Han; Chelsea Finn; Ankur Handa; Ming-Yu Liu; Donglai Xiang; Gordon Wetzstein; Tsung-Yi Lin
cotvla.problem: Robot manipulation from current RGB and language. Seven-dimensional end-effector/gripper actions and task-specific demonstrations differ from VLN navigation; future pictures are generated subgoals, not action-conditioned environment simulators.
cotvla.mechanism: Section 3 pp. 3–5 Eqs.2–3: first generate a future image from current image and instruction, then predict a short action chunk conditioned on that subgoal. VILA-U7B encodes 256×256 images as 16×16 positions with four residual codes each. Vision tower is frozen; language backbone, projector and depth transformer are trained. Causal visual-token CE (Eq. 4) plus full-attention action-token CE (Eq. 5) form Eq. 6. Each of seven action dimensions is discretized into 256 bins between training-data 1 st/99 th percentiles; ten-action chunks are predicted in parallel from special placeholders. Pretraining mixes selected OpenX robot data with action-free EPIC-KITCHENS and Something-SomethingV2 for visual targets; downstream task demonstrations fine-tune the same modules. Algorithm 1 generates subgoal, executes the chunk, obtains a genuine new observation and repeats. It does not observe intermediate outcomes during the whole chunk. The hybrid attention distinction affects latency and must be controlled separately from visual reasoning.
cotvla.novelty: Integrates visual subgoal generation and inverse action prediction in one autoregressive multimodal backbone, versus separate SUSIE generator/policy and direct OpenVLA action prediction. Its benefits may include action chunking, hybrid attention and additional actionless pretraining; visual imagination alone is not isolated by a comparison to a differently pretrained model.
cotvla.results: Table 1 p. 5 LIBERO average 81.13±0.6 versus OpenVLA76.5±0.6 across three seeds and 500 episodes per suite; Long 69.0 versus 53.7, Object 91.6 versus diffusion-policy 92.5. Thus not uniformly best. Bridge tasks use ten trials per task, and separate Franka models use 10–150 demonstrations per task (pp. 5–6). The abstract's relative gains should not be mistaken for percentage-point gains. No navigation experiment or independent execution. Table 3, p. 8 tests two novel tasks with five trials each: generated goal images yield 20%/0% success, while demonstration goal images yield 60%/40%. This small privileged-goal intervention supports a subgoal-quality bottleneck. Section 5 reports approximately sevenfold inference slowdown at chunk length ten due to generating 256 visual tokens, and acknowledges missing high-frequency feedback between chunk boundaries.
cotvla.bottleneck: Subgoals can be visually plausible but unreachable, and long chunks delay correction. Extra actionless data, backbone and full attention are material confounders. A good generated picture is not a calibrated physical counterfactual. Public project was located; complete released training/evaluation implementation not yet verified.
cotvla.followups: FantasyVLN imports visual CoT into navigation but uses it primarily during training, avoiding inference cost. WorldVLN interleaves real observation assimilation and predicted aerial video. These change the task and protocol, so their benchmark scores do not resolve CoT-VLA's manipulation failure modes.

cvaml.title: Calibrated Value-Aware Model Learning with Probabilistic Environment Models
cvaml.authors: Claas A. Voelcker; Anastasiia Pedan; Arash Ahmadian; Romina Abachi; Igor Gilitschenski; Amir-Massoud Farahmand
cvaml.problem: Model-based RL with stochastic transitions: should a learned model match full transition distributions or only value-relevant expectations? A sample-based value loss can unintentionally suppress transition variance. This is adjacent theory/continuous control, not a VLN algorithm or confidence-calibration method.
cvaml.mechanism: Sections 3–5: an (m,b)-VAML objective compares model value after m imagined transitions with a b-step bootstrapped real target. For independent real/model samples, Eq. 3 decomposes sample squared error into desired squared expected-value error plus model-value variance and target variance. The model variance term changes the optimum. CVAML subtracts an estimated model-value variance, requiring multiple model samples, to recover the intended expectation objective; finite-sample normalization must match the source implementation. The value learner is separately trained with ordinary TD (m=0) because stochastic MuZero-style imagined-target regression can fail even with perfect dynamics. Eq. 7 explains why latent feature MSE targets E[φ(s')] while value matching targets E[V (φ(s'))]; they commute for all distributions only with affine V. Proposition 5 gives existence of deterministic value-equivalent models under compact connected metrizable state space, continuous kernel/value and bijective latent mapping. It neither proves learnability nor guarantees arbitrary downstream rewards or policies. Training/inference otherwise inherit MuZero-style model-based RL agents; no picture generation is required. Appendix A.3, pp. 18–20, proves existence by continuity on a compact connected latent image and a measurable selection attaining the expected value. This supplies a measurable value-equivalent mapping for one fixed value function, not a continuous neural realization or a model preserving all language-conditioned values.
cvaml.novelty: Identifies a statistical bias in sampled value-aware model losses and supplies a correction, then separates model learning from value learning. Distinct from making visual predictions more realistic or estimating epistemic uncertainty. Closest predecessors VAML, MuZero and TD-MPC are explicitly analyzed rather than simply outscored.
cvaml.results: Figures 2–3 pp. 6–8 evaluate 1000 randomly generated Garnet MDPs with bootstrap intervals and seven challenging DMC dog/humanoid tasks with 30 seeds. Improvements depend on setting; not a universal dominance theorem. The finite-MDP experiments test the identified bias more directly than aggregate DMC return. No R2R/RxR or physical navigation validation is provided. Figure 4, p. 9 explicitly aggregates 30 seeds per environment. Appendix Table 2, p. 21 specifies latent width 512, batch 128, discount 0.99, actor/critic/model learning rates 3e-4, encoder rate 1e-4, one-step model rollout, and one/four model samples. Appendix C.4, p. 23 shows the BYOL-style auxiliary loss is essential in its humanoid experiments: objective calibration alone is insufficient.
cvaml.bottleneck: Correction requires extra samples and can increase estimator variance; value equivalence is policy/reward dependent, so preserving current V can discard information needed after a language-goal change. Existence conditions do not establish an implementable globally correct navigation model. Calibration here means objective correction, not action-risk reliability or conformal coverage.
cvaml.followups: DINO-WM and WoMAP use feature/dynamics losses; NavQ predicts successor semantics. A proposal about goal-dependent value calibration must distinguish CVAML's known sample-bias correction from a new navigation-specific contribution.

dinowm.title: DINO-WM: World Models on Pre-trained Visual Features Enable Zero-shot Planning
dinowm.authors: Gaoyue Zhou; Hengkai Pan; Yann LeCun; Lerrel Pinto
dinowm.problem: Offline action-labeled visual trajectories and a goal image. Zero-shot means planning toward new goals without reward-specific retraining; the transition model itself is trained. No language-route following is tested.
dinowm.mechanism: Section 3 pp. 3–5: frozen DINOv2 encodes an image into N spatial patches of width E, z∈R^(N×E). Embedded actions are concatenated with each patch; a Transformer with frame-causal attention predicts next patch features. Teacher-forced future-feature MSE (Eq. 1) trains the model; optional proprioception is concatenated. An independent pixel decoder can be learned with reconstruction MSE (Eq. 2), but planning does not need it. Inference uses receding-horizon CEM: sample action sequences, roll out latent predictions, score terminal feature MSE to the goal, refit elite action distributions, execute the first action and replan using a real image. Gradient-based planning is evaluated but weaker. Memory and compute scale with patch count, context and sampled rollout count rather than decoded image size.
dinowm.novelty: Uses frozen dense semantic visual features as a directly predictable state, avoiding reward learning and jointly learned pixel reconstruction; contrasts with PlaNet/Dreamer and global feature embeddings. Spatial patch ablations support the representation choice, rather than establishing universal pretrained-feature sufficiency.
dinowm.results: Table 1 p. 6: Maze/Wall/Reach/PushT SR .98/.96/.92/.90; comparison DreamerV3, retrained without reward,1/1/.64/.30. TD-MPC2 gets 0 in this reward-free setup, which is a task adaptation limitation rather than evidence the original reward-trained algorithm is universally inferior. Deformable Rope/Granular Chamfer distances .41/.26 versus Dreamer 2.49/1.05; sample sizes 50 for first four tasks and 10 for deformables. Table 2 patch versus CLS PushT .90 versus .44 supports spatial representation.
dinowm.bottleneck: Feature similarity need not equal task success; aliasing and counterfactual coverage can yield planner exploitation. A deterministic feature predictor averages multimodal outcomes. Repeated CEM rollouts impose compute, and no language, dynamic-obstacle or calibrated-confidence guarantee follows. These are methodological deductions from the representation and evaluation scope.
dinowm.followups: WoMAP adds language-conditioned distilled rewards and VLM action proposals. NWM changes latent representation to video generation. PiJEPA is a current language-conditioned planning lead for assignments 05–06.

dreamer.title: Dream to Control: Learning Behaviors by Latent Imagination
dreamer.authors: Danijar Hafner; Timothy Lillicrap; Jimmy Ba; Mohammad Norouzi
dreamer.problem: Learn continuous-control policies from images and scalar rewards with limited real interaction. It is reward-driven control, not language-conditioned navigation.
dreamer.mechanism: Section 3 pp. 3–5: recurrent state-space model has deterministic history and stochastic latent state; observation posterior is fit to a transition prior. World-model training uses pixel/reward likelihood and KL (Eqs.9–10), with contrastive/reward-only variants examined. From posterior states, imagination generates trajectories using the learned actor and transition model. Lambda returns (Eq. 6) combine truncated reward sequences with bootstrapped values. Actor maximizes these returns through differentiable/reparameterized dynamics (Eq. 7); critic regresses stop-gradient lambda targets (Eq. 8). Dynamics parameters are held fixed during behavior updates, while gradients propagate through their operations into actor actions. At deployment real images update the posterior and the actor selects an action; there is no online CEM tree search. Data collection, model fitting and imagined actor/critic learning alternate.
dreamer.novelty: Relative to PlaNet's per-step optimization, amortizes planning into an actor trained by analytic gradients through multi-step latent dynamics and value estimates. Compared with World Models, learning is joint/iterative and differentiable rather than CMA-ES over a small controller.
dreamer.results: Figure 6 p. 6 reports mean score 823 after 5 M environment steps across 20 DMC tasks, compared with PlaNet 332 and D4PG786 after 100 M; five seeds. The comparison supports sample efficiency in this suite, not equal compute or language navigation performance. Representation/return-horizon ablations show contributions, but no formal off-distribution guarantee.
dreamer.bottleneck: A policy can exploit model errors outside collected support; differentiable long rollouts can amplify model and value bias. Reward reconstruction can omit task-relevant details when future goals change. The learned policy removes online search cost but shifts cost into imagined training and an imperfect value model.
dreamer.followups: DreamerV2/V3 extend representation/scaling; NavMorph imports RSSM dynamics into VLN. CVAML later shows value-aware stochastic-model loss pitfalls; these are related but not a claim that original Dreamer uses every analyzed loss.

planet.title: Learning Latent Dynamics for Planning from Pixels
planet.authors: Danijar Hafner; Timothy Lillicrap; Ian Fischer; Ruben Villegas; David Ha; Honglak Lee; James Davidson
planet.problem: Continuous control from 64×64 images and rewards, without state access during acting. Learns a latent simulator from online data and plans actions through it.
planet.mechanism: Sections 2–4: RSSM deterministic history h_t=f (h_(t−1),s_(t−1),a_(t−1)) and Gaussian stochastic state s_t; posterior conditions on current encoded image, prior on history. Pixel/reward likelihood and prior-posterior KL form variational objective (Eq. 3). Optional latent overshooting compares multi-step transition priors with observed posteriors (Eqs.5–7), stopping posterior gradients for distances>1. Crucially p. 5 states final RSSM does not require overshooting. MPC/CEM samples Gaussian action sequences, predicts latent rewards, selects elites/refits distribution for several iterations, executes the first action and replans from the new posterior. No pixel decoding is needed inside planning, and there is no learned actor/value network. Random seed experience is followed by planner-collected experience and repeated model updates.
planet.novelty: Combines deterministic and stochastic recurrent state with online latent MPC; extends latent generative dynamics beyond one-step reconstruction. Overshooting is a methodological contribution but should not be falsely described as essential to every reported RSSM result.
planet.results: Figures 4–5 evaluate sixDMC tasks and show importance of combining deterministic memory and stochastic states. Reported sample-efficiency comparison with model-free agents uses different compute and interaction budgets. These experiments support compact latent planning on their suite, not calibrated model probabilities or VLN performance.
planet.bottleneck: Planning cost scales with candidate sequences×horizon×iterations. A single stochastic rollout per candidate is a noisy score, and selecting high predicted reward can exploit model errors. Longer imagined horizons compound model bias; limited observation history can alias hidden states.
planet.followups: Dreamer amortizes planning into an imagined actor; DINO-WM removes reward and pixel-decoder dependence through pretrained features; NavMorph applies RSSM to language navigation. All shift tradeoffs rather than proving model correctness.

worldmodels.title: Recurrent World Models Facilitate Policy Evolution
worldmodels.venue: NeurIPS 2018; related World Models arXiv version
worldmodels.problem: Learn compact visual models and evolve a small controller; test whether a controller can learn in a hallucinated simulator and transfer to a real environment. CarRacing and VizDoom are not instruction-navigation benchmarks.
worldmodels.mechanism: Sections 2–4: VAE maps pixels to z; MDN-RNN predicts a Gaussian-mixture distribution over next z from current z, action and recurrent h. A small linear controller maps concatenated[z,h] to actions and is optimized by CMA-ES with episodic reward. VAE/RNN are pretrained separately on 10,000 random rollouts without controller reward. In CarRacing, controller evolution evaluates real environment trajectories using compact features. In VizDoom, a learned termination predictor and MDN-RNN form a simulator in which the controller is evolved before real transfer. Sampling temperature controls stochasticity. It is not per-step online imagination search and the two experiments use different training deployment arrangements.
worldmodels.novelty: Demonstrates compact model-based representation and entirely dreamed controller training with transfer, using separable perception/memory/control. The architecture is simple enough to expose exploitation of the learned simulator directly.
worldmodels.results: Table 1 p. 4 CarRacing fullVMC906±21 versus vision-only 632±251 over 100 trials. Table 2 p. 4 Doom at temperature .1: virtual 2086 versus actual 193 survival steps; at 1.15 virtual 918 versus actual 1092. Section 4.2 p. 6 explicitly documents controller exploitation of model deficiencies. This is concrete evidence against treating visually plausible simulated success as physical success.
worldmodels.bottleneck: Policy-induced distribution shift exposes world-model inaccuracies; low-temperature models can be exploited. Increasing temperature is a useful empirical heuristic, not calibrated uncertainty or a general robustness proof. Random pretraining may omit important actions/outcomes; the small controller also limits expressiveness.
worldmodels.followups: PlaNet/Dreamer iteratively collect policy experience and learn stronger latent behavior; CVAML clarifies value-aware model objectives. The exploitation bottleneck survives architecture changes and requires evidence from actual outcomes.

lookbeforeleap.title: Look Before You Leap: Bridging Model-Free and Model-Based Reinforcement Learning for Planned-Ahead Vision-and-Language Navigation
lookbeforeleap.authors: Xin Wang; Wenhan Xiong; Hongmin Wang; William Yang Wang
lookbeforeleap.problem: R2R instruction navigation with six low-level actions and RGB features. Learns visual/reward predictions to augment a model-free policy rather than relying only on history-conditioned action selection.
lookbeforeleap.mechanism: Sections 3–4 pp. 4–9: instructionLSTM and ResNet152 image features feed model-free policy. Two MLP environment models predict next visual feature and progress reward (Eqs.2–3). For each of five non-stop first actions, a depth-two imagined trajectory is encoded by anLSTM; these rollout features are concatenated with model-free context before final policy scoring. Train environment predictors first by feature/reward MSE using 95%teacher and 5%random actions, then freeze them. Policy learning mixes supervised imitation and REINFORCE, with annealed teacher weight. Reward is geodesic distance reduction D (s)−D (s')(Eq. 10), requiring simulator supervision during training. At inference short feature rollouts are repeated at each real step. Algorithm 1's printed annealing expression uses exp (iter/T) despite 'decrease'; the intended negative sign cannot be assumed without source confirmation.
lookbeforeleap.novelty: Early navigation-specific hybrid of imagination-augmented decision making and imitation/RL, prior to later pixel/NeRF/latent systems. Imagined features directly affect inference but do not form a persistent global map.
lookbeforeleap.results: Table 1 p. 12 unseen SR 24.6 versus cross-entropy 21.3 and model-free 21.5; test 25.3 versus 22.1/23.1. Gains establish proof of concept under this early action interface, not modern baseline competitiveness. Model and policy ablations matter more than cross-era score comparisons.
lookbeforeleap.bottleneck: Teacher-heavy environment data poorly covers the policy's mistakes; a frozen predictor cannot correct subsequent shifts. Fixed short horizons and deterministic features obscure multimodality. Additional real observations correct history but there is no explicit model-risk estimate or test-time residual update.
lookbeforeleap.followups: DREAMWALKER replaces feature-only branches with explicit future panoramic imagery; HNR predicts features efficiently in continuous navigation. Neither should erase this earlier model-based inference prior art.
